article.overview: An ultraviolet telescope is an instrument that collects ultraviolet (UV) light from celestial objects and records it as images or spectra. On the Moon, such a telescope would sit on the surface, outside the dense part of Earth's atmosphere and with no atmosphere of its own to absorb most of the signal. Two surface instruments have been operated so far. The Apollo 16 Far-Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph observed the Large Magellanic Cloud and Earth's upper atmosphere in April 1972 [1][2]. The Lunar-based Ultraviolet Telescope (LUT) on China's Chang'e-3 lander has operated since December 2013 and is described by its team as the first robotic astronomical telescope working on the lunar surface [3][4]. Several further lunar UV designs have been proposed but, on the evidence gathered here, have not flown [5].
article.description: A lunar ultraviolet telescope combines a mirror or lens system, a UV-sensitive detector and a pointing mechanism. The optics bring light from a small patch of sky to a focus, where a detector records it. Because UV light is more strongly absorbed by materials than visible light, the optical coatings and detectors are chosen for the UV band, and the optics must be checked for performance at those wavelengths. The Moon's slow rotation means that a fixed telescope sees the sky drift past slowly, while a steerable mirror can hold a star or galaxy in view for longer. The two flown instruments used different approaches. The Apollo 16 camera was a hand-aimed, film-recording instrument. LUT is a robotic instrument with a gimbal-mounted pointing mirror, a CCD detector and remote operation [3][4].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a lunar UV telescope is to observe bright UV sources that are hard to study from Earth. The LUT team lists two main science goals: to monitor bright variable stars in the near-ultraviolet band continuously for up to about a dozen days, and to carry out a sky survey at low Galactic latitude in the near-ultraviolet, covering regions that the GALEX mission avoided [3]. The Apollo 16 team used its instrument to image the Large Magellanic Cloud and to record spectra of early-type stars and interstellar extinction [1]. Their analysis also used the instrument to observe Earth's upper-atmosphere glow [2]. The LUT team's aim of monitoring a target continuously for up to about a dozen days [3] shows why a stable surface platform is attractive for time-domain work, although the lunar night limits how long any one site can observe.
article.operating_principle: The three operating principles below differ in detail, so each flown or proposed example is described separately. Apollo 16 camera. The instrument was an electrographic Schmidt camera with interchangeable correctors. The LiF corrector admitted wavelengths of about 1050 to 1600 Å, and the CaF2 corrector about 1250 to 1600 Å [1]. A grid collimator set the field of view in the spectrographic mode, which recorded spectra over about 900 to 1600 Å and 1050 to 1600 Å [1]. The images and spectra were recorded on an emulsion, which was later scanned with a microdensitometer and converted to intensity values after calibration [1]. The electronographic principle, in which ultraviolet photons are converted to electrons that expose the recording film, is general background and is not separately sourced here. LUT. LUT uses a Ritchey–Chrétien telescope with a 150 mm aperture and a focal ratio of F/3.75. A fixed flat mirror folds the light to a Nasmyth focus, where a two-lens field corrector and a UV-enhanced 1024 × 1024 frame-transfer CCD with 13 µm pixels are located. A gimbal-mounted pointing flat mirror aims the telescope, with a designed pointing accuracy of 0.05°. Two LED lamps at 286 nm provide an internal flat field [3]. LUCI (proposed). The LUCI design uses an all-spherical optical layout to avoid the aspheric mirrors needed by Ritchey–Chrétien telescopes. The authors describe it as a cost-effective and simple solution [5].
article.scientific_importance: The Moon offers a stable, airless platform for astronomy. The Chang'e-3 team describes the Moon's very slow rotation and extremely tenuous atmosphere as advantages for long, continuous observations [3]. The Apollo 16 and LUT results have shown that a lunar-surface UV telescope can produce usable data, and the LUT photometric calibration showed stable performance over time [4]. These results show that a surface UV instrument can be built and operated, but they do not show whether a surface observatory is more cost-effective than a space-based one. That comparison was not assessed in this draft.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a lunar ultraviolet telescope. The instruments that have been built differ in optics, detector, mass, operating mode and mission context, so their numbers are not directly comparable. The examples are listed by status: one historical instrument that operated on the Moon, one robotic instrument reported as operating in the published record, and one proposal.

examples.name: Apollo 16 Far-Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph
examples.status: Flown; operated on the lunar surface, 21-23 April 1972
examples.description: The Naval Research Laboratory's Far-Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph (Experiment S-201) was operated on the lunar surface during the Apollo 16 mission, 21-23 April 1972 [1]. In the direct imaging mode it covered circular fields of about 20 degrees in diameter, with a limiting resolution of about 2 arcminutes at the centre and about 4 arcminutes near the edges [1]. Exposures were taken with a LiF corrector (1050-1600 Å, up to 10 minutes) and a CaF2 corrector (1250-1600 Å, up to 30 minutes). Spectrographic exposures ran for up to 30 minutes in the 900-1600 Å range and up to 200 minutes in the 1050-1600 Å range [1]. The Large Magellanic Cloud sequence began at 17:18.5 UT on 22 April 1972 and ended at 23:20 UT the same day [1]. Secondary sources report that the instrument was a tripod-mounted, f/1.0, 75 mm electronographic Schmidt camera with a mass of 22 kg [6]. These values were not verified against a primary document in this draft and should be treated as unverified until checked against the Carruthers 1973 Applied Optics instrument paper [2]. The film cartridge was returned to Earth; the remainder of the package was left on the lunar surface [6]. The Smithsonian's record for a reconstructed backup unit is listed in secondary sources but was not accessed in this draft.

examples.name: Lunar-based Ultraviolet Telescope (LUT), Chang'e-3
examples.status: Flown; operating on the lunar surface since December 2013 according to the published record
examples.description: LUT was developed by the National Astronomical Observatories of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (NAOC) and the Xi'an Institute of Optics and Precision Mechanics (XIOPM). It was launched on 2 December 2013 on a Long March-3B rocket and had its first light on 16 December 2013, two days after the Chang'e-3 landing [3]. Published characteristics: Ritchey-Chrétien telescope; aperture 150 mm; focal length 563 mm; focal ratio F/3.75; field of view 1.36 degrees by 1.36 degrees; UV-enhanced 1024 x 1024 frame-transfer CCD with 13 µm pixels; pixel scale 4.76 arcseconds per pixel; designed pointing accuracy 0.05 degrees; NUV coating transparency peak at 2500 Å with effective width 1080 Å [3]. Over its first six months, LUT acquired more than 50,000 images [3]. The magnitude zero point was 17.54 ± 0.09 mag (set A) and 17.52 ± 0.07 mag (set B), with no detectable variation between the three standards observed for three to four runs each [3]. An 18-month analysis gives a zero point of 17.53 ± 0.05 mag, using 17 IUE standards in 51 runs, and reports stable performance over the whole period [4]. The mass of LUT is not given in the published sources reviewed here and is recorded as not publicly specified. Secondary reporting states that the telescope's lifetime was expected to be about one year, that it has run for about 2000 hours and observed about 40 stars, and that the telescope doors close at the day-night boundary to limit lunar dust [7]. The primary 18-month paper instead describes the cabin as closed at both sunrise and sunset, with the telescope initially mounted inside the Chang'e-3 lander cabin, and credits these measures for avoiding dust-related degradation [4]. The secondary claims about operating hours and doors are not verified and are not relied on here.

examples.name: LUCI, Lunar Ultraviolet Cosmic Imager
examples.description: LUCI is a near-ultraviolet imaging instrument design by a team whose authors include Mathew, Prakash, Sarpotdar, Safonova, Murthy and Brosch [5]. The authors describe it as an all-spherical design that could fly on high-altitude balloons, nanosatellites or larger missions. The payload is reported as weighing below 2 kg, and it is designed to survive launch loads [5]. The paper is part of a series titled Prospect for UV observations from the Moon. The abstract refers to a future spacecraft to the Moon as part of India's entry in the Google Lunar XPRIZE competition [5]. No aperture, focal ratio, detector format or field of view is given in the abstract reviewed here. Its 130-180 nm wavelength band appears in secondary summaries and was not confirmed in the abstract; the abstract itself describes the instrument as near-ultraviolet. A separate proposal, described in an SPIE paper from 2022, envisages a 20-30 cm UV telescope for the International Lunar Research Station, with a slewing mirror and switchable filters and detectors [8]. That proposal was reviewed only from a search-result summary and is listed as a concept.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Apollo 16: secondary sources report a 75 mm, f/1.0 electronographic Schmidt camera, not verified against a primary document. LUT: 150 mm aperture, 563 mm focal length (F/3.75) [3]. LUCI: not specified in the abstract reviewed.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Apollo 16: secondary sources report 22 kg, not verified. LUT: not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. LUCI: reported as below 2 kg [5].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed for any of the three examples.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar surface telescope must survive a long night and a long day, each about 14 Earth days [9]. NASA's Diviner-based analysis gives daytime temperatures near the equator of about 120 °C (400 K) and nighttime temperatures of about −130 °C (140 K) [9]. The Moon has no atmosphere to moderate these extremes [9]. The Apollo 16 observations were made in April 1972 [1]. LUT's published record covers 18 months of operation, which spans many lunar day-night cycles, and the team describes the cabin arrangement as helping to avoid dust-related degradation [4]. Operationally, the telescope must be able to point and track a target while the Moon rotates. LUT's gimbaled pointing mirror is designed to a pointing accuracy of 0.05° [3]. Calibration requires standard-star observations. The LUT team used observing runs close to 30 minutes so that a star moved relative to the fixed stray-light pattern, which allowed the stray light to be modelled and removed [3]. Power, data-link and thermal-control requirements for these instruments are not described in detail in the sources reviewed here and are recorded as a gap.
article.limitations: The Apollo 16 instrument produced film-based data from a single mission and a single set of targets. Its published specifications come largely from secondary sources in this draft. LUT has a small aperture of 150 mm and a field of view of 1.36° × 1.36°, so it surveys a small patch of sky at a time. Its published data are calibrated photometry, and its images contain a stray-light background that the team had to model and remove before photometry [3]. The LUCI and ILRS-type designs are proposals and have no flight heritage.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Apollo 16 and LUT both reached the Moon as surface instruments, but the published sources describe their transport and deployment only in outline. The LUCI and ILRS-type concepts are proposals with no verified lander interface.
transportation_process: Apollo 16: carried to the lunar surface on the Apollo 16 mission and operated there [1]. Secondary sources state that the astronauts carried and aimed the instrument by hand and that the film cartridge was returned [6]; these details are not verified against a primary mission document.

LUT: carried to the Moon on the Chang'e-3 lander. It was first mounted inside the lander cabin, and the cabin was closed at sunrise and sunset, which the team credits with avoiding dust-related degradation [4].

LUCI and ILRS-type concepts: proposed for a lunar mission. The LUCI abstract refers to a future lunar spacecraft in the Google Lunar XPRIZE context but does not name a lander [5]. No lander or spacecraft compatibility is asserted.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo 16: hand-aimed by the astronauts according to secondary sources, not verified. LUT: gimbal-mounted pointing mirror on the lander-mounted telescope; the mechanical and thermal interfaces with the lander are not described in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 16 Far-Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph (1972) [1][2]; Chang'e-3 Lunar-based Ultraviolet Telescope (2013 onward) [3][4].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted, because verified interface evidence was not found for any of the examples.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 16 instrument produced far-ultraviolet imagery and spectra from the lunar surface. Its results include images of the Large Magellanic Cloud at about 3 arcminutes resolution in the 1050-1600 Å and 1250-1600 Å ranges, and spectra of the region [1]. The instrument was designed by George Carruthers and the Naval Research Laboratory team and was described in a 1973 Applied Optics paper [2]. LUT is significant as the first robotic astronomical telescope working on the lunar surface, according to its developers [3]. Its long-term photometric stability results are an early test of how a surface telescope behaves over a year or more [4].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- The Apollo 16 mass, focal ratio and aperture values (75 mm, f/1.0, 22 kg) come from secondary sources and have not been verified against the 1973 Applied Optics paper [2][6].
- The Apollo 16 film-based data from a single mission cannot be directly compared with modern CCD photometry from LUT.
- LUT's mass is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
- Secondary reports of LUT's operating hours (2000 hours), number of stars observed (40) and dust-door arrangement are not verified against primary sources; the primary 18-month paper describes the cabin arrangement [4][7].
- The wavelength band (130–180 nm) given for LUCI in secondary summaries is not confirmed by the abstract reviewed [5].
- Whether LUCI or any ILRS-type telescope has flown has not been established; the sources reviewed describe them as proposals.
- General background statements (the electronographic technique, UV absorption by Earth's atmosphere and by materials) in the Overview, Description and Operating Principle sections are not separately referenced.
- No verified images were added to this article; image assets were not checked against official pages in this run.
